title: Tokens and the two phases of LLM inference

opening.headline: The cost and speed of LLM services can be read in terms of three concepts: tokens, input processing, and output generation.
body: The same words always appear in the LLM API's bill and response time. Input token, output token, time to first response, cache. If you don't know what these words refer to, numbers seem like rules to be memorized. Conversely, if you know the order in which your model processes requests, the same numbers tell a story.

In this class, we will look at what tokens are, how a model reads input all at once and writes output one token at a time, and why recalculation can be avoided by storing the internal state created in the process. It deals with principles that apply to any service, not the settings of a specific product.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what tokens are and how input and output tokens are counted respectively
This can explain why the step of processing input all at once and the step of generating output one token at a time operate differently.
This explains what can be avoided by storing the internal state (KV state) of the front part of the processing, and why there are limitations to that storage.
It can explain why the cost and response time configurations of requests with long inputs and requests with long outputs are different.

screens.title: The number of characters is similar, but why are the cost and speed different?
screens.lead: Read the two requests and think about what makes the difference between cost and response time. This screen is for reading only.

visual.alt: Schematic comparison of request A with long input and request B with long output as bars.
labels: Request A: Give me a long document and summarize it in one line
Request B: Ask short questions and write a long report
Where will the cost and time come from?

paragraphs: A team sends two types of requests: Request A asks for a long document to be pasted in its entirety and summarized in one line. Request B sends one short question and asks you to write a long report. The number of characters on the screen for both requests may be similar.

However, when you open the invoice, the input and output are counted separately, and the response time appears to be different for the two requests. It takes a while for the first letter of A to appear, but once you start, it's over in no time. B gets the first letter quickly but takes a long time until the end.

Three things are needed to explain this difference. These are the tokens, which are the units in which the model reads and writes text, the fact that the stages of reading input and writing stages behave differently, and the internal state created during reading. This class solves these three things one by one.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If billing and response times are based on something other than character count, what are those criteria? I'll answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me start from what I already know: experience.

screens.title: Think about it: How writing is made
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen answers appear one after another on the chat screen, rather than all at once?
items.answer: This is exactly how the model actually creates text. The model does not create the entire answer at once, but builds it one token at a time from the beginning. The speed at which bits and pieces appear on the screen is the creation speed.

items.prompt: Have you ever pasted a very long document and asked a question, and it took an unusually long time for the first letter to appear?
items.answer: Much of that latency is spent reading long input. The model must first process the entire input before writing an answer. Typically, the longer the input, the longer it takes for the first letter to appear.

items.prompt: How many tokens are there in one Korean sentence? Will it be the same as the number of characters?
items.answer: There is no set value. A token is neither a letter nor a word, but a unit of fragments used by a model, and the same sentence is broken down differently for each model. So the length should be measured in tokens, not in characters.

screens.outro: So, let’s start with what exactly a token is.

screens.title: Token: A unit of data that the model reads and writes.
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: LLMs read and write text in units of token, not by characters or words. A token may represent a full word, a portion of a word, or a fragment including punctuation or whitespace. A component that defines the rules for splitting text into token units is called a tokenizer, and these rules vary by model. The side sending the request to the model uses input token for counting, while the side receiving the response from the model uses output token for counting, and both are reflected in usage metrics. There is a limit on the number of token units a model can process in a single request, and this range is referred to as the context window. It is estimated that English sentences contain roughly four token units per sentence, though this is only an approximation, and ratios may differ for other languages such as Korean. Therefore, when determining fees and limits, text length is not counted; instead, the service's coefficient function is used to check the number of token units. Even this value is an estimate, and actual billing is based on the usage volume contained within the response.

terms.tip: This is the basic unit of text that the model processes. Sometimes it's a single letter, sometimes it's a single word, sometimes it's a part of a word. The number of characters and the number of tokens do not match.
This is a rule that divides text into token pieces. Each model has different rules, so the number of tokens in the same sentence may vary depending on the model.

This is a token count of system instructions, conversation transcripts, tool definitions, pasted documents, etc. that are sent in the request. This includes everything the model reads before answering.
This is the number of tokens that the model generates and returns. In some services, tokens used for internal, invisible inferences are also counted as output.
This is the upper limit on the number of tokens the model can handle in one request. Usually, input and output share this range together.

screens.outro: Now that we know what a token is, let's step through how the model processes them and in what order.

screens.title: Inputs are read all at once, outputs are written one token at a time.
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see the two steps in sequence through which the model processes one request.

visual.alt: A two-step flow chart in which input tokens are processed all at once, followed by output tokens one by one.
labels: Store the internal state of each token
The previous token must exist to create the next token.

steps.title: Step 1: Process all input at once
steps.body: When a request arrives, the model first reads the entire input token. Since the inputs are all already given, we can compute the tokens all at once, side by side. At this stage, the model creates internal state for each input token and is ready to pick the first output token. This step is often called input processing, or prefill in English.

steps.title: Step 2: Output is generated one token at a time in order.
steps.body: The output is different. The model selects a new token, concatenates the tokens, and then selects the next token. Because each output token depends on all inputs and all outputs created so far, they cannot be sequenced or created simultaneously. This step is often called output generation or decode in English, and this generation method is called autoregressive generation.

steps.title: The new token references all previous tokens
steps.body: When choosing a new token, the model looks at the information of all tokens before it. This calculation that considers the relationship between preceding tokens is called attention, and is the core of the Transformer structure used in LLM today. Each time you create a token, you need to refer to the entire previous part, so if you store the calculation results from the previous part somewhere, you won't have to recalculate them from scratch every time. This storage unit is in KV status in the following screen.

steps.title: The two stages create different times
steps.body: Input processing takes longer for longer inputs, which affects the time it takes for the first letter to appear. Output generation takes one step each time a token is created, so the longer the output, the more time it takes to complete. This is why output generation often accounts for the lion's share of the overall delay of a request. If the input is long, such as a summary, and the output is short, the first letter will be completed quickly at the latest, and if the output is long, such as writing a report, the first letter will take a long time to finish at the earliest.

steps.title: Costs are also divided into two categories.
steps.body: Most API price lists separate the unit prices of input tokens and output tokens, and set the output unit price higher than the input unit price. It is each service that sets the unit price, but it is helpful to understand this pricing structure that output is done step by step, making it difficult to use processing equipment efficiently. Exact unit prices and rates vary for each service, so check the price list.

screens.outro: Now, let’s take a look at exactly what the internal state we created earlier is.

ext.title: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180)
Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017, arXiv:1706.03762)

screens.title: KV status: Memory of previous part of processing
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what internal state the model created earlier and why it is kept there.

tabs.label: something
tabs.body: When the model reads input tokens, it creates two sets of numbers for each token: a key and a value. Afterwards, when creating a new token, the keys and values ​​of the previous tokens are called and referred to. This collection of numbers is called the KV state, and the stored value is called the KV cache. What is stored are calculated numbers, not letters or previous answers.

tabs.label: Why keep it?
tabs.body: Without archiving, each time you create a new token, the keys and values of all preceding tokens will have to be recalculated from scratch. The longer the output, the greater the waste. If you save it, you only need to recalculate the key and value of the new token and read the rest. This is reuse within one request.

tabs.label: Things change when the future changes
tabs.body: The key and value of a token depend on all tokens preceding it, not just that token. Even with the same token, different states are created depending on what is in front of it. So, if the first part changes even by one letter, all states after that point must be recalculated. The only way to reuse state is to repeat the same part of the state.

tabs.label: Takes up memory
tabs.body: The KV state grows with each token, taking up significant memory. In one studied example, an OPT-13B model with 13 billion parameters consumed approximately 800 KB per token and up to approximately 1.6 GB per request. These values ​​are examples that vary depending on model scale. Memory is limited, so state cannot be stored forever, and services place limits on storage time. This is why cache entries have a lifetime.

tabs.label: Expand across requests
tabs.body: When the next request with the same prefix comes, the saved state can be reused. Cost and first response time are reduced by skipping the processing of earlier inputs and processing only the new ones. This is how prompt caching works. Here comes the condition that the first part must be exactly the same in each token and come back within the storage time.

screens.outro: Now that we've outlined the principles, let's take a look at how cost and time vary depending on the shape of the request.

ext.title: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180)

screens.title: Shape of request and composition of cost and time
screens.lead: Move the sliders to change the appearance of your request to see how your cost and response time changes.

stops.body: This is a summary or classification request that reads a long document and responds briefly. The input token accounts for most of the cost, and a lot of time is spent on input processing, but the output is short, so the overall process ends quickly.

This is a request to write a long article with short instructions. Input processing ends quickly, so the first character comes out quickly, but since there are many output tokens, both cost and completion time are incurred in the output.
This is a request to read long material and write a long report. Both the time to first letter and the time to completion are long, and both input and output costs are high.

These are requests where the same long instructions are prefixed to each request, only the questions are changed. Keeping the KV state at the front allows skipping input processing, reducing cost and first response time even when input is long.

screens.outro: Now let's apply all these concepts at once with a numerical example.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Are requests with 80 times longer inputs more expensive?
screens.lead: Solve by comparing the two requests using the numbers assumed by the instructor. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. Unit price rates are assumptions for illustrative purposes only and are not actual service values.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Request A gives a document with input of 8,000 tokens and receives a summary with 200 tokens. Request B gives a short question of 100 tokens as input and receives a report of 2,000 tokens. The input length of A is 80 times longer. For cost comparison, assume the output cost is 5 times the input cost.

steps.title: Step 1: Divide costs into inputs and outputs
steps.body: If the input unit price is 1, A multiplies 8,000 by 1 and adds 200 by 5, which is 9,000. B adds 100 multiplied by 1 and 2,000 multiplied by 5, which is 10,100. A, which has an input 80 times longer, is actually slightly cheaper. Cost is determined not only by input length, but also by the balance of input and output and the unit cost ratio.

steps.title: Step 2: Divide time into input and output
steps.body: A takes a long time to read 8,000 tokens, so the first letter appears late. However, the input is processed all at once and the output is 200 tokens, so it ends soon. B requires very little input processing, so the first letter comes out quickly, but the 2,000 tokens have to be created one by one, so it takes a long time until the end. The overall completion time is likely to be longer in B.

steps.title: Step 3: When the previous part is repeated
steps.body: Assume that A is repeated several times for the same document, only changing the questions. If the document has the same front page every time, you can keep the KV state you created the first time and reuse it. Starting with the second request, we skip processing the input of 8,000 tokens and only process the new question, reducing both cost and time to first letter.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: The questions about reducing cost and speed always come in the same order. Is the input long, is the output long, and is the first part repeated? If the input is long and repetitive, state reuse is effective, and if the output is long, reducing the output or choosing a faster configuration is effective. The same principles explain caching, lazy decomposition, and price tag reading.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Input, Output, Storage
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read it while remembering the question you asked at the beginning. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Let's go back to the original question. Bills and response times are driven by the number of input tokens, the number of output tokens, and whether previous state can be reused, not the number of characters. Because input is read all at once and output is written token by token, the two parts contribute to cost and time in different ways.

Take a look at whether the service you use takes up the lion's share of input or output, and whether there is a repeating front part for each request. The answer will tell you which optimizations will be effective.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the best reason why requests with long output take so long to complete?
options: Output tokens can only be created one at a time, so the number of steps increases in proportion to the length.
This is because the output is always processed by a model that is larger than the input.
This is because the output token is not compressed when transmitted over the network.
Unlike input, output has a predetermined length and is created at once.
checks.explain: Each output token depends on all of the inputs and outputs created so far, so they cannot be created simultaneously; they proceed step by step. So the completion time increases almost proportional to the output length.

wrong.1: The output and input are not handled by different models. The same model performs both steps.
wrong.2: Transmission compression is not the cause. The key to the delay is the generation method that produces the tokens in order.
wrong.3: The output is not produced all at once, but one token at a time.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Output proceeds in order because the previous token must exist to create the next token.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The reason the output is long and slow is because of how it is created, not the model or transmission. Recall that output tokens are created sequentially, one at a time.

checks.intro: Make sure you have sorted out the nature of your KV status. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: When can the stored KV state be rewritten in the next request?
options: If the new request is similar in meaning to the previous request
When the first part of the new request continues token by token exactly like the previous request
If the new request has the same length as the previous request
The same word is used the same number of times in the new request.
checks.explain: The state of one token depends on all tokens before it. Therefore, only the state of the parts that are the same from the front can be used as is, and if the front changes, the rest must be recalculated.

wrong.0: Even if the meaning is similar, if the tokens are different, the status will be different.
wrong.2: The same length does not mean the same state.
wrong.3: Even if the number of words is the same, if the order and location are different, the status is different.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Since the state depends on the previous tokens, only the parts that are identical from the previous one can be reused.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Similarity, length, or number of words are not criteria. Think about it in terms of the fact that the state of each token depends on all the preceding tokens.

right: Completion time and cost arise primarily from output length.
This is because the tokenizer cuts the text into different pieces for each model.

glossary.def: This is the basic piece unit for a model to read and write text. It does not match letters or words, and usage, fees, and limits are all calculated based on the number of tokens.
This step is to read all input tokens of the request at once to create the internal state of each token. The longer the input, the longer the time until the first response.
This is the step of creating output tokens one by one in order. The longer the output, the longer the time to completion increases almost proportionally.

The numerical bundle of keys and values calculated for each token at the beginning is called the KV state, and the one stored to avoid recalculation is called the KV cache. This is not a post or answer, but a calculation result.
This is the upper limit on the number of tokens the model can handle in one request.

misconceptions.myth: Tokens are like words and can be approximated by the number of characters.
misconceptions.fact: Tokens are pieces determined by the tokenizer and do not match words or letters. Since the ratio varies depending on the language and model, the length must be checked using the counting function provided by the service to check the number of tokens.

misconceptions.myth: Since output is processed all at once like input, its length has little effect on time.
misconceptions.fact: Input can be read all at once, but output must be produced one token at a time in order. So the longer the output, the more the completion time increases almost proportionally.

misconceptions.myth: The KV cache stores previous question and answer sentences.
misconceptions.fact: What is stored is the result of calculating the key and value obtained by processing the preceding token. Responses are generated anew for each request.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The model reads and writes token by token rather than character, with input and output tokens counted separately.
Inputs are processed all at once, and outputs are generated one token at a time in order.
Recalculation can be avoided by storing the internal state (KV state) of the processed part, but storage is limited because it takes up memory.
Cost and time vary depending on the input length, output length, and whether the previous part is repeated.
closing.reflectionLead: This is a question to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Are the requests I'm running closer to the long input side or the long output side? How much of the first part is repeated the same in each request?
